prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep B007 as a single-part prize and I have not changed my configuration since round 1. The chair's summary shows that six members hold it, but I note that several of us, myself included, arrived there after reading the openings, so the count carries no weight in my judgement. What carries weight is that the scientific case survived every reservation raised. The magic-wavelength condition is one sharp idea: it makes the trapping potential invisible to the clock transition and so removes the light shift as an obstacle for a many-body ensemble. Katori conceived and demonstrated it. Ye's programme then turned a concept into the most accurate and most stable frequency standard, and into a platform where collective and spin-correlation effects in a lattice of atoms are controlled and measured. Independent laboratories (RIKEN, JILA, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) agree at the 1e-18 level, which is the kind of confirmation that settles maturity. The two-name attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist. As a statistical physicist I read the achievement as the systematic suppression of noise and systematic shifts in a quantum many-body system, and that is a physical result and not merely an engineering one. On the chair's question about wording, I think a citation that names the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice, and not clock accuracy in general, separates this from the comb and ion-control recognitions.
statement.case_against: The reservations are real and I do not dismiss them. The overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems is a matter of judgement: a committee could read lattice clocks as a very good continuation of recognised metrology. Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and Lisdat are not credited, and a two-name prize will be criticised from that side; I can defend it only because the concept and the record-performance programme are the decisive steps and no third person has an equally compelling claim. The redefinition of the second is still pending, so part of the impact is prospective. Finally, B005 is at least as original in scale, and my reasons for not preferring it are about maturity and credit, not about quality. If those two obstacles were removed, I would find the choice between B007 and B005 genuinely hard.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B005 with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, pairing the 2011 flat-band prediction with the 2018 observation, and argues that robust, widely reproduced phenomenology suffices even though the pairing mechanism is unsettled, with the citation kept to the phenomena.
responses.response: I take the point that a wording confined to the prediction and the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states avoids claiming a mechanism, and I accept that this reduces my first objection. It does not remove the second one that you also list yourself: Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 experiments, cannot be named, and a citation that credits the observation to two others will be read as unfair whatever its wording. The three-name limit makes this omission structural, and I think the committee should not accept it when a cleanly attributed candidate of high quality is available. I do not claim that B005 is premature in the sense of being wrong; I claim that in a few years the field will have settled the mechanism and the credit chain better, and the prize will be easier to defend. My ranking of B005 as the first alternative stands.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B005 as an exemplary prediction-plus-experiment story, compares the unresolved mechanism to high-temperature superconductivity in 1987, and flags her own field proximity to moire physics as a possible bias.
responses.response: The 1987 analogy is fair as far as it goes: the cuprate prize was awarded for the discovery, with the mechanism then and now unresolved. But that discovery had a single, unambiguous experimental origin and a short credit chain, which is exactly what is missing here. Twist-angle disorder and sample dependence, which you and Olsson raise yourselves, also mean that what is intrinsic and what is device-specific is still being sorted out. I value that you disclosed the proximity, and I do not read your preference as biased; I simply weigh maturity and attribution more heavily than the scale of the opened field. Where we agree is that B005 is an outstanding candidate and that it is the principal competitor to B007.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, supports B007 as a genuine instrumental invention reproduced by several groups, flags the Cao omission as a substantive obstacle for B005, and does not favour B043 as a second part.
responses.response: I agree on the Cao point and on B043, and I take your reservation about the pending redefinition of the second as the right one to keep on the record. On a two-part prize I would go further than you: I do not see a second candidate that is clearly distinct from B007 and cleanly attributable. B012 has the credit-arbitrariness problem I described, and your own note that the source associations are at the 3-4 sigma level supports waiting. Adding a second part would dilute a clean prize in order to include more people, which I do not think is a scientific argument.

responses.point: Johansson moved from B044 to B007 and says the citation must be worded so that the lattice concept, and not clock accuracy in general, is what is rewarded, given the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
responses.response: I agree with the wording requirement and have written my citation accordingly: it names neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength and the 1e-18 level, and it does not speak of clocks in general. I would add that the ion-clock lineage of 2012 relies on a different physical principle, a single trapped ion with minimal perturbation, whereas the lattice clock relies on interrogating many atoms at once with the light shift engineered away. That difference in principle, and the many-body effects that follow from it, is why I consider B007 a distinct achievement and not an extension of the earlier prizes. Your disclosure regarding B044 is handled appropriately by your own proposal to discount your view there.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B007 as precision measurement at its most fundamental, wants a clean two-laureate prize, opposes adding a third name, and prefers pairing only with a clearly distinct achievement.
responses.response: I agree that no third name should be added. I looked again at whether Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde or Lisdat could displace either laureate, and I find that they could not: Katori holds the concept and the first realisation, Ye the record-accuracy and many-body programme. The others made important contributions that are real but sit on top of these two. I also agree with your condition for a second part, and by that condition I find that none of the other shortlisted candidates qualifies this year, so I leave it as a single part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct in principle from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes it prudent to wait; I judge that the physics does not depend on it, but I cannot exclude that a majority will.
Whether the omission of Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and Lisdat can be defended publicly, even if the internal argument for two names is sound.
Whether the B005 credit gap (Cao) and the open mechanism will be resolved soon enough that B005 becomes the stronger case next year.

My own B025 case (two-dimensional melting and the hexatic phase) remains on my list for its intellectual depth, but I do not claim that it is mature enough in distinctness from the 2016 prize to be preferred now.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has changed since round 1. None of the credited names on B007 or on the other shortlisted candidates appears among my documented co-authors, supervisors or institutional connections. My field (statistical physics of complex systems, with an interest in neural networks) is adjacent to none of the shortlisted topics in a way that I regard as a source of bias, but I note that I come to the many-body and noise aspects of B007 as a theorist and not as an experimentalist.
